The Assembly

Seven parts become one machine. FreeCAD gives you two ways to do it, and they suit different jobs.

The Assembly01 / 08

Pick deliberately

Two ways to assemble

Joints

  • You pick a face on one part and a face on another, and FreeCAD holds them together.
  • This is what SolidWorks calls a mate.
  • Good for anything that has to line up, or move.

Links

  • You place a copy of a part at a position you give it.
  • One link object can hold a whole list of positions.
  • Good for repeated parts on a regular spacing.

Nine tynes on a regular pitch is exactly the second case. With joints that would be eighteen separate mates to create and keep in step.

The Assembly02 / 08

Save before you link

Starting the assembly

Three things to get right before you place anything.

  1. File › New, then save it immediately
  2. Open each part file you are going to use
  3. Switch to the Assembly workbench
  4. Insert the frame first and leave it at the origin

Save first. A link stores the path to another file. Until your assembly has a path of its own, FreeCAD cannot work out a relative one, and you get “owner document not saved”. Everybody hits this once.

The Assembly03 / 08

Design parts around their interfaces

Placing nine tynes

Both tynes were modelled with their mounting face at zero height, centred on their bolts. So placing one is two numbers.

RowAcross the machineFront to back
Front, 5 off−38, −19, 0, 19, 38−10 in
Rear, 4 off−28.5, −9.5, 9.5, 28.5+10 in

That is the payoff for choosing the part origin carefully back in Deck 3. Had the origin been at some corner of the bounding box, every placement would carry three corrections and a rotation.

The Assembly04 / 08

Check it from above

The stagger

The rear row sits half a spacing across from the front row. That is the whole trick.

  • Both rows are at 19 inch pitch.
  • The rear row is shifted 9.5 inches sideways.
  • Seen from the front, the nine points are 9.5 inches apart across a 76 inch swath.

Check this view before you go further. If the points are not evenly spread, the offset is wrong — and it is much easier to see here than in an isometric view.

The Assembly05 / 08

Placements have limits

The blades and the braces

Each sweep sits at its tyne's point. The tyne's tip position comes straight out of the part model.

These are placements, not joints. Move a tyne and its blade does not follow. A Coincident joint between the tyne's point face and the blade's top face would keep them together properly.

For a picture it does not matter. For a machine you intend to keep changing, it does.

The Assembly06 / 08

Joints

Doing it with joints instead

Worth doing once by hand, because a joint tests something a placement never does: whether the parts actually fit.

  1. Assembly › Create joint › Coincident
  2. Click the underside of the tool bar on the frame
  3. Click the top of the tyne's mounting head
  4. The faces snap together. The tyne can still spin.
  5. Add a second joint on a bolt hole of each to stop it

Do this once and you will find out whether your bolt holes line up. On this machine they do, because the frame's 3 inch spacing and the tyne's 3 inch spacing came from the same reading of the tutorial.
